Words of comfort and suggestions for the house. Poverty worries her.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My daughter for ever,

  1. I received your letter this morning and I am very sorry about the sad news you give me. My daughter, it seems that in these days troubles are raining down from every side. I pray God to hold my head steady so that I do not go mad.1 What am I to say? Only that this is happening because of me: there are my sins!!

  2. Courage,2 let us trust in God, and he, as it is his Work, will provide for everything.

  3. This morning, as soon as I received yours, I wrote again to Signor Della Valle and another letter to the Superior3 (all the way here). Now I have done my part; God will do the rest.

  4. Meanwhile let us bless this dear Eternal Father for giving us Fr. Luigi, who is a real support and wholly devoted to the work of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate.4

  5. As for the mattress you mention, do as you think best. I wrote to Maria again and sent the letter to Albaro.5

  6. I see you are upset about the bills; but, daughter, believe me, it is good for this Priest to know everything; I myself, you see, spoke to him about our temporal affairs. I hope that once you have talked to him about it, you will find it very easy to do what now repels you.6

  7. You complain that I do not write to you. But if you saw my occupations,7 which give me no peace night or day, you would surely stop complaining. Just listen: what if I told you that my head has to travel a thousand miles a minute! So many people with nothing. All living on providence.8 I am in a position to say with Saint Paul: Lord, I can bear no more.9

  8. Try to look after yourself, and then you can go and call on the benefactors to see if you can collect something. I fear I may have to set out on some journey to get a few provisions for the winter.10 If only God would once show this unhappy woman what he wants.

  9. Courage, daughter: a brief suffering for a great joy. One day, when we are up there among the blessed — if by God's mercy this creature gets there — our suffering will seem little, and we will be sorry we could not bear more for love of our God.

10. Jesus, with his breast bared, will show us his wounds, and then, blushing because we have nothing to dress them with or cover them, we will be filled with pity; and [for] us, who always seek our own good, they will surely be a great pain.

Greet all the sisters for me and believe me, ■

your poor Mother Rosa G.

1 She takes on the problems of the Family, especially those of the superiors. She not only suffers with them in empathy but even feels responsible for the troubles that rain down from every side, and attributes them to her sins.

2 Courage! In comforting the sister she rekindles her faith and finds again, in trust in God, a clear view of her action: for God's Work, with boldness in hope.

3 The two Vincentian priests who were the community's spiritual guides.

4 In this priest's selfless, active presence the Mother welcomes a providential gift from the dear Eternal Father, a help both comforting and practical. He is a real support and wholly devoted to the Work of Saint Anne. These words reveal her deep intuition of the gift of belonging to the holy Mother's Family, shared with «friends», especially priests. Later, in 1887, five priests of the Neapolitan clergy would try to found the religious Congregation of the Sons of Saint Anne. Cf. Frati R., Virga Iesse, no. 4, 1986.

5 As the letters show, her friendship with Maria d'Annenkoff developed as a mutual gift of help in faith and in love for God and Saint Anne, in her Work.

6 Francesca found it hard to reveal to outsiders the

community's serious financial problems, whereas the Mother considered Fr. Luigi one of the family.

7 My occupations. Of hands and of everything. Not only are they so many that they take all her time every day, but they worry her so much that she wears herself out mentally in the difficult, vain search for solutions.

8 With nothing. No fixed income, in total, trusting reliance on providence and on the generosity of people of goodwill and kind heart.

9 I am in a position: in the situation.

10 She herself will have to go round asking for donations and getting some provisions for the winter.

She gives news and entrusts her with some errands.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My daughter,

  1. I am worried, because I have had no more news of Fr. Luigi's health. We are praying constantly here; send me news at once.

  2. Today I received two letters, one from the Superior and the other from Signor Della Valle; they assure me that they will always direct you1 and that he will see about sending someone else while Signor Della Valle is in the country. Tell Fr. Luigi. Go and thank them both in my name.

  3. I wrote to Federico about the shed.2 If you can, send me the fringe, for charity's sake. You go and pester Federico too;3 then we will get something. Nothing more for now. Goodbye.

In haste, I am your poor Mother Rosa

Greet everyone for me, and God bless you. A thousand respects to Fr. Luigi.

1 Cf. Letter 237, n. 3.

2 Cf. Letter 208, 2. Work to repair it had been going on for some time. Cf. Letter 204, n. 7.

3 Go yourself too and insist in person.

She teaches her the need to follow Jesus in the mystery of his passion and resurrection, like Mary.

A.M.F. My Francesca,

  1. Today I received your letter full of anguish; what am I to answer? Only that1 [for] whoever wants to follow Jesus, this is the way: suffering and pain. These are the torments of our Master, the pains and the most cruel agony which, one may say, began on the first day of his passion.

  2. Daughter, one can stay on Tabor only to take a little rest, and Jesus wants to take weak souls there, for if he does not refresh them they die on the way. But the strong go ever onward,2 spurred on, until they reach Golgotha, and there, crucified with him, they rise all beautiful and radiant and enter triumphant into the glory of heaven.

  3. Mary, Mary! On Monday, daughter, behold the Mother of sorrows. Who more than you, fairest among all peoples, suffered the anguish, the cruellest heartbreak a Mother's heart could endure? Now all the heavenly legions together do not make up a fraction of your beautiful, most resplendent light; a single ray of yours is enough to light up all heaven.3 What do you think: is it better to rejoice, or better to suffer?4

  4. I leave the choice to you. Answer me, and consider whether what this poor Mother of yours tells you about suffering is true: that inside it there is a most delicious, savoury honey; learn to taste this fruit and you will see that you can never have your fill of it.

  5. Come, courage;5 you will soon see the Lord comfort you; but an ounce of patience and two of faith in God, and you will have everything, I assure you. But peace, and little quibbling. Day by day embrace the cross

the Lord sends us. Remember: new days, new crosses.

6. I enclose a letter for Sr. A. Giovanna's brother. ^b ^At the end of the month go and collect 100 francs, and as soon as I have a penny I will give you a share.

If you think you should approach the Archpriest about the matter you know of, do so. This evening I wrote to the Superior to thank him, and also to Signor Della Valle and to our Fr. Luigi. I will write to Federico7 too, to hurry him up.

  1. Greet Fr. Luigi and everyone for me. On Sunday I will answer all the letters from the other daughters that I have not yet answered. Meanwhile, God bless them, and may you be flooded8 with his blessing, so that you may be filled with consolation and strength. Try not to be distressed.

  2. Here is the medicine I am sending you for your stomach. Take a little magnesia9 now and then, and oil to anoint yourself.

Pray often, and have others pray for me.

Believe me your poor Mother Rosa

1 There is only one answer: for whoever wants to follow Jesus, this is the way. Suffering and pain means placing oneself under the sign of the Master's cross.

2 Strong souls go ever onward. The cross is a road leading to Calvary, to crucifixion with Christ and to being raised with him in glory. Mother Rosa, who had offered herself as a victim of reparation and in her spiritual life had conformed herself to Jesus' physical sufferings, including through penitential instruments and practices, trains her daughters to follow Jesus by accepting daily pains and sufferings willingly and joyfully and giving themselves unreservedly to the service of charity in God's Work for the poor, the sick and girls in difficulty.

3 Monday, 15 August, feast of the Assumption. The Mother of sorrows now shines in heaven with «most resplendent light».

4 An invitation to a responsible, free choice: Tabor or Calvary? Answer me. It calls for careful reflection to test the truth of what she says. In this way she can learn to taste the sweetness of suffering for love and will never be satisfied.

5 Come, courage! A rousing exhortation, with the reassuring certainty of her deep maternal intuition, which wants and sees her daughter fulfilled in complete joy: the Lord will comfort you. But on one condition: your cooperation. And she mixes its ingredients: an ounce of patience, two of faith in God, peace, no quibbling, loving acceptance of each day's new cross.

6 Sr. A. Giovanna Bixio.

7 To her brother Federico, to hurry along some work on the house.

8 The blessing from God that she implores is a generous outpouring of peace, happiness and saving strength.

9 Magnesia, and anoint your throat with blessed oil.

Piacenza. Mother House. Mother Rosa's little room.

She comforts her, sharing her sufferings, and tells her of the opening of a new house in Piacenza.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My blessed daughter,

  1. Two lines, to add a word of comfort, drawn from the depths of my own grief.2 Courage, my daughter. God wants us so; let us kiss his hand in the hour when he strikes us. I am with you and share your pain,3 and when I add to it all the afflictions the Eternal is pleased to send me in these blessed days, I assure you, my daughter, I can hardly believe a human creature can bear them; this gives me strength, seeing that God, our beloved all, protects and helps us amid so many trials, under which our human nature alone would surely give way.

  2. If it pleases God, we will open another house, as you will hear from Fr. Luigi.4 Then on my way back I will come and see you. Yesterday, or rather the day before, the Municipality gave me the house you know of, near the parish priest of the Paganina.5 Not the one opposite ours any more, but another, and [in] it there will be about thirteen nuns6 and two rooms for the boys' schools. But we must wait for the tenants to leave, and they are good people and will leave soon. Tell the sisters, for it will be a great comfort to us.

  3. My Franceschina, what troubles over Maria!7 This crowns the work. What do you say? Instead of being a relief to the house, she is an enormous burden. She leaves tomorrow. Silence about this, for charity's sake.

Send me news of your health often.

I am your poor Mother Rosa

1 The date is derived from the notice of the Municipal Council's decision sent to the parish priest of Santa Maria dei Pagani in Piacenza, Strada della Morte, Fr. Elia Magnani.

2 A word of comfort. Not mere words but the support of spiritual consolation, the gift and fruit of unspeakable, extreme grief. Saint Paul expressed the same experience to the Corinthians: «as we share abundantly in Christ's sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too» (2 Cor 1:5).

3 In empathy she joins her Franceschina's afflictions (note the diminutive!) to her own countless ones, and in the depths of her extreme, failing weakness she touches God's protecting strength, «our beloved all». If I add up all the sorrows of these days, it seems impossible to me that a human being could bear them.

4 Fr. Luigi had become the confidant of Family matters. Because of his love for the work of Saint Anne she considered him one of the household.

5 The Mother was on excellent terms with the parish priest, given her deep sense of the Church (cf. Arch St FSA, Pos. Foundations).

6 On 17 September a formal municipal deed was drawn up granting use of the municipal house in Strada Morte for nine years, for the infant school and the boys' school. It was handed over on 20 November 1870 (Arch St, ibid.).

7 Maria d'Annenkoff. She had initiative and, in her own way, offered suggestions that were sometimes untimely and at odds with the Mother's views (Arch St FSA, Pos. Friends).

A.M.F.

My Superior,

  1. This letter will be handed to you by our excellent benefactor, Signor Giuseppe Brigidini.1 He will give you news of the whole house and a small parcel. There is no need to commend him to you, for however much we might do, it will never be enough to repay him.2

  2. If you have not yet sent the fringe, you can give it to him.

Goodbye. Many greetings to all, and believe me, your

poor Mother Sr. Anna Maria Gattorno

1 Signor Giuseppe Brigidini also undertook to sell the cloth woven at the Mother House. Cf. Letter 224, 2.

2 We shall never be able to repay all the good he does us.

She gives news of her health and asks for news of Fr. Luigi.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My blessed daughter,

  1. Now the time of famine is over and abundance has come at last.1 I got up only a few hours ago, after a violent headache until 11 that was splitting my skull; it had come on at midnight.

  2. I am very happy to be able to say to the Lord: «I offer you a little suffering in return for that most cruel suffering you endured from those terrible thorns, which were the work of my sins».2

  3. Now I seem like a being that lives without knowing it is alive;3 everything rings in my ears like a distant sound. Blessed be God, who wants us to live like this, feeling the blows of his most holy Hand.

  4. You cannot imagine how distressed I am about Fr. Luigi. Today the Father is having a novena begun specially for him, that the Lord may restore him to health quickly and fully, so that he can work for God's works.

  5. I hear the sister4 is so unwell. I await news, which I hope will be good. Every train that arrives we say: here is Fr. Luigi; but it never is, only bad news.

  6. I would like you to get this letter into Maria's5 own hands, and to know whether she received my other one, whose date I no longer remember; I think it was last Friday. It was very long.

  7. I wanted to write to all the sisters, but time is short and I must send these by the consignment6 that is leaving.

  8. I hope to send you tomorrow everything you mention. I am sending you 25 francs for the fringe and tassels.7 Greet Fr. Luigi for me. Tell him to write and tell me how his health is, for I am truly worried.

Goodbye. The Lord bless you and all of them.

I am your poor Mother Sr. A. M. Rosa

9. P.S. This is the third time I have written to you this week; I think you will not cry any more, now that you are living in abundance.

1 A playful reference to the letters she has written her: three in one week.

2 I am very happy. She faithfully lives her share in Jesus' sufferings, seizing every chance to offer something, always small compared with his agonising pains.

3 Her descriptions of her medical conditions are always vivid.

4 Sr. A. Addolorata Gianni (cf. Letter 245). 5 Maria d'Annenkoff.

6 Luggage consignment.

7 The tassels.

She asks for financial help for the Sampierdarena community, which is in extreme want.

A.M.F. All God's,

  1. I received your letter, but it did not satisfy me at all; I want to know whether we will be going to the house we are negotiating for, and I want you to pray.1 Whether the Lady I spoke of is that one, whether Providence will come, and when. My good daughter, the poor house of Sampierdarena is so short of means that it lacks everything and does not know what to do; for charity's sake, give them a mite of yours; I beg you, truly weeping for those poor creatures. Yesterday and today the Superior no longer knows what to do. Believe me, my good daughter, God will reward you.

  2. Forgive me for being so bold; but what can I do? When I am in despair, when there is no means of meeting their needs, every little makes a lot.2

  3. I am sending you the book;3 it is only one, but poverty will have it so. Patience. Write me something good. Tell me lots of things, for I long to hear them. For charity's sake, say nothing about what I write to you; burn this letter under obedience. Come, for I want to speak to you. Tell Rosa4 to pray and to break with avarice and send me some word, and God will reward her. I would write more, but I feel really ill. Last night I thought I was dying.

Goodbye. I am your

poor Sr. A. M. Rosa

1 She was negotiating with the Municipality of Piacenza for a house to be used as a school. Cf. Letters 204, 5; 240, 2.

2 Small contributions go a long way towards meeting their needs.3 Cf. Letter 110, 1.

4 Rosa Parodi.

She answers questions about the school and gives advice and encouragement.

A.M.F.

My good daughter,

  1. I have received your letter, and this [evening], although I am sleepy, I am making an effort to answer you. First. About the school,1 tell the mothers this: they are to come on the first day of November to enrol their little girls. Put them in the room just inside the entrance. As for the boys, tell Signora Morando to let it be known that the Reverend2 no longer wants to give us the schools, and you will say: «we would gladly take them, if we had room».

  2. But for us now patience is needed. We are truly under attack on every side. My daughter, go to that gentleman and commend yourself to him; go also to Fr. Angelo of the Remedy3 and commend yourself to him too.

  3. I keep forgetting to tell you that the Father sent Teresa Merlano4 away, and now [she] wants her shawl, which you have there. See if you can find it, and then, when I write to you,5 send it to her; but say nothing, for charity's sake.

God bless you, and believe me

Your most affectionate Mother Rosa

  1. In haste. Do not worry so much about the priest.6 God will provide; I hope that if you pray you will have the Spiritual Exercises in a few days, and then you will be comforted a little.

  2. I hope, if I can, to come and attend them. I will soon send you the girls' dresses; I hope by Saturday.

Goodbye. I am as tired as a donkey and cannot write any more. Read it as best you can, for it is very badly written.

Greet all the sisters for me. God bless you.

1 The Institute ran an elementary school for day girls.

2 The Rev. Fr. Angelo Ricchini, Letter 208, 1.

3 Cf. Letter 207, 5.

4 Teresa Merlano's dismissal is also recorded in the Novices' register.

5 When I let you know her address.

6 The priest who had been staying in the house as chaplain had left.

Francesca is ill and must come urgently to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our holy Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Our daughter,2

  1. I have just received your letter and heard the bad news about my Franceschina. If you can put her on the journey, do so at once, as soon as you receive this.

  2. You are to come with her, bringing broth and everything needed. I am also writing to Fr. Luigi, and I hope he will agree with me.

  3. Come at once.3 Tomorrow evening I will be expecting you without fail. This morning a novena begins, and let us hope the Lord will heal her. Give her a little of the oil I sent you, by mouth. In short, bring her at once. I would come myself, but I cannot; come, under obedience.

  4. Keep a close eye on those who have recovered from smallpox,4 so that they do not go where the little girls are, because it is during recovery that it is usually passed on. For charity's sake, do not let the girls see them. And the same with Addolorata.5 Anoint her too, and pray, for we are praying here.

Goodbye. The Lord bless you.

I am your poor Mother Rosa

1 It is addressed to Francesca but actually speaks to one of the Sisters of the community who had sent her the news.

2 It is Sr. A. of the Good Shepherd Bastia, the vice-superior.

3 At once... at once; come... come. Mother Rosa's tenderly maternal anxiety and concern for this most faithful daughter and co-worker in God's Work is evident. Give her a little blessed oil.

4 A precaution of great importance for hygiene.

5 Use the blessed oil for Sr. A. Addolorata Gianni too.

She is very busy, but if her presence is needed in Piacenza they must call her at once.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My good daughter for ever,

Blessed be our holy Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Yesterday I did not answer your half-sheet, because just as I sat down to write to you the French nun arrived;3 after her two people from Cremona, then the lady from Ferrara, then the Father, who, poor man, also had his share of work. And then a visit from Fr. Paolo and other short visits, as if they had all agreed to come yesterday.

  2. Reading your letter I shuddered.4 My God! How can it be? Patience! If you and the Delegate think my presence is needed, do not spare me.5 I would rather come in time, while things can still be put right, without having to struggle for breath.

  3. So think it over, reflect, and then, if you think fit, call me. You know I must be here for 7 September and will not be free until the 22nd of that month. And then6 I can stay with you until mid-October, for yesterday I learned that the Countess will be away only for that time. Tell all this to the Delegate for her guidance.

  4. I hope you are better. My daughter, believe that this unworthy Mother of yours always prays for her beloved daughter. Courage, silence; let no one know your affairs. Keep quiet.

5. The girls' uniform dresses would be better hung up. You could ask Fr. Luigi to buy a wardrobe without a back7 to hang the dresses in, and you can put it in the passage8 that leads down to the girls, you know, near the door of the Delegate's room. Do you understand? That is enough for now; tomorrow I will write again, and meanwhile I will answer the Delegate.

God bless you, and believe me always yours. I am in a hurry

Most affectionate Mother Sr. A. R.

1 This letter was found among Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni's correspondence, but it certainly belonged to Francesca, who had been in Piacenza since 27 August for treatment. The Mother suggests that, once back in her community at Sampierdarena, she have Fr. Luigi buy a wardrobe. She addresses Francesca and the delegate Adelaide Pezzoni in the plural; Adelaide was surely given the letter to read and kept it.

2 It is dated to the end of August because of the reference to 7 September in no. 3.

3 The French nun: a friend she had met through Maria d'Annenkoff, who corresponded with the Mother. She signs her letters Soeur Marie Grégoire; she was a Trinitarian. Cf. Arch St FSA, Pos. Friends.

4 Shudder.

5 Do not spare me the strain of the journey; I would rather come in time, so that the situation can be remedied, than be forced to rush in afterwards to repair the damage, out of breath. There is not enough evidence to work out what problem had been reported to her.

6 And then. From that date I can stay there until mid-October, since yesterday I learned that the Countess (it cannot be said who) will be away only for that time.

7 Without a back. With no back panel.

8 A passageway; a Genoese expression.

She teaches her about self-love and its effects, the love of God and the spirit of prayer.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Our daughter for all time,

  1. A little time, and I am devoting it all to you; by this you will see that this poor Mother of yours never forgets her little girl.

  2. Little girls are extremely dear to Jesus; but do you know what kind of little girls Jesus loves? Simple, humble ones, who because they are small do not yet have that monster of self-love, which belongs to the old self.1

  3. The Virgin Mary too, because she also loves little doves,2 likes little girls and loves them dearly, because pride and its sister vainglory have not yet grown in them. They may be a little vain, but that is only the smoke their senses give off from having been formed when they put on creaturehood.3

  4. Let us begin with the first, which we may call our governor, self-love,4 truly a tree which I believe springs up in us as soon as the slightest sense of mere movement forms in us; and when the heart is formed, it puts down its first roots there and spreads them, making itself master of all our intellectual faculties.

  5. Only one counterweight can bring it down, overcome it with its powers, take possession of it and alone hold sway: the love

of God, our all. Whoever possesses it can say with certainty that every human power has been dispersed.5

  1. You will reply: «How does one acquire it?» We must do as good pilots do, who always keep the compass turned to the pole and never trust either favourable winds or a calm sea, leaving the boat to the helm alone. A storm comes up, and there is the ship tossing among the waves, out of [control], heading for the rocks. So it is with souls who abandon the compass of prayer, which points straight to the pole, the centre to which they refer,6 that is, God. From there they receive true direction and are always united with that good pilot, our Saviour, who brings us without shipwreck to a harbour of salvation.

  2. Through prayer everything is received. Whoever sets his mind7 to pray attentively and fervently, vocally, soon through fervour gains the prayer of union and of quiet; from there passes to meditation, from meditation to contemplation, and so on, etc.

  3. Now let us turn to our actions. You will say: «In this blessed position of mine, always busy with a thousand tasks, always amid so much temporal business, how can I find recollection in prayer?» I will answer8 that Saint Teresa, while holding a frying pan in her hand, went into ecstasy, pan in hand. God the Father is very pleased while we are at work; indeed I tell you we have a better means of charming him,9 because when we act truly intent on doing that work for him alone, he takes such delight in us that he is charmed.

  4. Oh! Blessed the soul that succeeds in charming its Beloved, the Eternal, its all!10 Two spouses charmed with each other. No other thought reigns in them but to do everything that pleases the beloved; the Bride will satisfy her Beloved Jesus by doing everything for him and accepting every cross,11 and indeed she will always try to relieve him of the one others lay on his shoulder. And what will this Sovereign Spouse do for his Beloved? What gems, of what value, will his gifts be, what delicious, lovely sweets!

I have no more time.12 Goodbye. I am

your very poor Mother Rosa

1 Belongs to the old self. Disordered love of self is characteristic of

the old self, which lives according to the flesh and not according to the spirit (cf. Rom 8:5-8).

2 The Virgin Mary too delights in little doves, that is, girls endowed with «dovelike simplicity» (cf. Mt 10:16; Rule of 1869, ch. 1, virtue of simplicity).

3 This expression, like all the others in the letter, is unclear. The smoke the senses give off because of original sin when, at conception, they became human creatures.

4 Our governor, self-love, a tree, as the source, because of sin, which shows itself in the branching of the «capital vices» and the many disordered desires connected with them.

This tree, I believe, springs up in us as soon as we perceive the sense of movement, and when the heart is formed it puts down its first roots there and then spreads them, becoming master of every activity moved by the intellect.

5 Only a contrary force can bring it down and overcome it with its powers, take possession of it and rule it: the love of God. Whoever possesses it can say that every sinful human power has been weakened.

6 To which they refer. The pole of their one constant point of reference.

7 Whoever sets his mind to pray enters the dynamism of the spiritual life towards the Lord, along a path of progressive stages: vocal prayer, meditation, the prayer of quiet and of union, contemplation. Mother Rosa refers to these stages and, after writing, put them in order by adding numbers above the words.

8 You will say..., I will answer. To the objection she expects from Adelaide, who did not passively accept advice, she replies with a vivid, apt and effective illustration from the life of Teresa of Avila, from whom she took the stages of prayer set out above.

9 Charm him. Draw him to us with pleasure, delight, joy.

10 Blessed the soul. With logical consistency she goes on to describe the bridal love of Creator and creature celebrated in the Song of Songs, which she knew through Saint John of the Cross, whose works she owned. Vol. II, containing the Spiritual Canticle, the Living Flame and other works, ed. P. G. Fassi, Como 1859, was found after her death and is still in her little room in Piacenza.

11 Accepting every cross. This is the very personal key feature of her spirituality: receiving every cross from him as a personal, reparatory sharing in his Cross, in an all-embracing relationship of love.

12 I have no more time. She wrote in one burst, carried away by spiritual fervour, and breaks off abruptly, as in other letters, with a hurried goodbye.

She asks her to send cloth for making mattresses and some personal belongings of sisters recently transferred. She gives advice about the house and commends the little girls and Carlotta to her.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our holy Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Our daughter,

  1. I have received all your letters, and from your reply1 I see you did not understand me properly. I did not say you did not deserve a letter from me; no, I only meant that, as I had many things to tell you, those two lines were only to calm your suspicions.

I will turn to God and beg him to fill you with graces. And be sure that if the Lord hears my prayers, you will be repaid in all your desires.

  2. The Lord is testing poor Carlottina with the anguish of certain illnesses for which, as far as I can judge, the doctors can find no human remedy. She is seized by continual vomiting, which went on for some twenty days. For a few days now it has given her a few hours' respite,2 and she is beginning to eat; poor thing, how sorry I feel for her, for to see her suffer like this, and so little understood,3 truly grieves anyone who sees her; her consolations have been changed into suffering and dryness, and at first she could find no peace; now she is resigned and suffers with great resignation.

  3. I would tell you something of my health, but I can say it all in one word. It no longer exists; only a skeleton walking about. There are days when I have not the strength to stand, a real donkey of the Lord's; for when the time comes to set out or to work in new houses, the good God gives me as much strength as I need to stay on my feet.

  4. I hope to come to Rome. How much it is needed, Father Agostino! This poor community lacks many permissions, especially for Holy Week, to hear Mass on all three days, that is, to have the Holy Sepulchre.4 My God, with so many and such large communities, I assure you it grieves me greatly to see them deprived of so great a good. Teach me, Father Agostino, a way to obtain everything.

  5. And then there is the approval of the Rules. So you see whether

my desire to come there is small. This grace I ask of the Lord: to have the good fortune before I die of seeing them approved. A few days ago the Bishop here5 promised me to see to them and approve them.

  1. Father Agostino, why do you say nothing about the hope that you would come here? Could you not make the journey after the holidays? You should come; I assure you it would do so much good. Come and see another new house here in Piacenza, where 100 boys are taught, all of them ringleaders of the city, and there are 20 religious too. All this on providence.6

  2. Certainly there are days when, from thinking so much, I feel my brain rotting. And the same with the Genoa house:7 there are already seventy and perhaps more, because there too they increase every day. They have had the good fortune to find the Vice-Parish Priest well disposed towards them, and a very learned and wise Religious acts as chaplain and, one might say, as servant.8

  3. I hope I have obeyed your order to write you a long letter, which I fear will bore you to read. In your reply tell me you are coming after Epiphany.

Commend me to Our Lady, and bless me;

I am your very poor Sr. A. M. Rosa Gattorno

II. INDEX OF RECIPIENTS OF THE LETTERS

  1. BIXIO (Sr. Anna) GIOVANNA, born in Genoa on 10 May 1816. A widow. She was one of the first five followers of Mother Rosa Gattorno who left Genoa for Piacenza on 13 March 1866. She received the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne on 8 December 1866. She died on 26 February 1891.

  2. BOSCO (Fr.) GIOVANNI. Saint. Founder of the Salesians and the Salesian Cooperators and, with Saint Maria Domenica Mazzarello, of the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians. Born at Becchi (Castelnuovo d'Asti) on 16 August 1815. Ordained priest in 1841. Died in Turin on 31 January 1888.

  3. CAMISA (Sr. Anna) FRANCESCA. Born at Cortemaggiore (PC) in 1846, she entered the Daughters of Saint Anne on 1 February 1867 and received the habit the same year. Knowing her excellent qualities and gifts and her human and religious maturity, Mother Rosa made her superior in communities which were then all newly founded. She was superior at Cento (Ferrara) for almost a year (1867), then at Sampierdarena (1868-1870), at Piacenza, house in Via della Morte (1870-1872), at Piacenza, Mother House (1872-1874) and finally at Sampierdarena, in the hospital community (1874-1875), where she died on 8 September 1875, aged 29.

  4. CAMISA (Sr. Anna) MARIA LUIGIA, sister of Sr. A. Francesca, whom she had preceded in choosing religious life among the Daughters of Saint Anne, entering the Institute on 20 November 1866 and receiving the habit on 8 December 1866. She was superior of the Mother House (1867-1869) and then of the Cento community for a few months.

She did not prove worthy of the Foundress's trust. As superior she abused her authority and in March 1869 went so far as to plot against her with the aim of ousting her. She left the Institute on 4 August 1869. Cf. lett 83; 89; 125; 126; 133; 138.

5. CAMPANELLA ADELAIDE, mother of Mother Rosa. Born in Genoa in 1802, she married first Gerolamo Ravano, by whom she had a daughter, Amelia. Widowed very young, she married Francesco Gattorno, by whom she had six children: Emanuele (1828-

1873), Rosa (1831-1900), Giustina (1833-1917), Federico (1836-1913), Elisa (1838-1919), Francesco (1843-1922). She died in Genoa on 18 December 1882.

  1. CAMPANELLA (Prior) GEROLAMO. Born on 25 January 1806, he was ordained priest at Savona in July 1828. In 1839 he was appointed Prior of the Parish of Our Lady of Carmel. A priest of great faith and charity, he concentrated his ministry on his parish, with a preference for the poor. A friend of Fr. Giuseppe Frassinetti, he gave him hospitality in his small villa at S. Cipriano in Val Polcevera when both had to leave Genoa in 1848 for political reasons. In 1869 Mother Rosa asked him to make available to the home-nursing Sisters the house he wished to offer for social works. Cf. lett 109.

  2. CARACCIOLO ISABELLA, daughter of Count Giuseppe and of Lucrezia, of the Counts Villa-Maruffi. She did not marry and, like her brothers Francesco and Maurizio, devoted herself to charitable works. She died in Piacenza in 1880.

  3. CARACCIOLO (Countess) LUCREZIA, née Villa-Maruffi, married Count Giuseppe Caracciolo. She was widowed in 1865. She was known for her kindness and for her gifts to the needy and to charitable institutions, among them the Daughters of Saint Anne. She died in Piacenza on 21 December 1870.

  4. CHARVAZ (Mgr.) ANDREA, bishop of the Diocese of Genoa. Born at Moûtiers in Savoy on 25 December 1793 [original: 1893], he followed a priestly vocation. He took a degree in moral theology in 1817 and taught in the seminaries of Moûtiers and Chambéry. From 1825 to 1833 he was tutor to the sons of Charles Albert, Victor Emmanuel and Ferdinand. In 1833, designated by Charles Albert under the Concordats then in force, he was consecrated bishop of Pinerolo, but in 1847, when the king in one of his constitutional reforms subjected religious and ecclesiastical writings too to civil censorship, he resigned and retired to his native Savoy.

Later King Victor Emmanuel, to resolve a serious situation of friction with the Holy See, proposed to Pope Pius IX the appointment of his former tutor as bishop of the diocese of Genoa. He accepted only out of obedience in faith to the Pope, and for 17 years (1853-1869), very difficult times, he was an outstanding model of a pastor. In August

1869, for health reasons, he asked to resign and was allowed to. He died the following year, on 18 October, at Moûtiers.

  1. CONSOLINI (Cardinal) DOMENICO, born at Senigallia (Ancona) on 7 June 1806. Cardinal Deacon of S. Maria in Domnica, Chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church and Arch-Chancellor of the Roman University. He died in Rome on 20 December 1884.

  2. CUSTO ALESSANDRO, son of Gerolamo and Rosa Gattorno. Born in Genoa on 28 October 1855. He attended regular courses at various colleges run by religious but did not complete them, because at 18 he wanted to go into business, following the family tradition. He sought his fortune in Argentina, in vain, in partnership with a cousin, but had to return to Italy sadly disillusioned, having met in less than a year with hardship and bankruptcy. Life in Italy was not easy for him afterwards either. He died in Piacenza aged 36, on 16 March 1891.

12. CUSTO CARLOTTA FRANCESCA MARIA, eldest child of Gerolamo and Rosa Gattorno. Born in Genoa on 8 December 1853. Struck by a childhood illness, she lost her hearing and so was educated from 1864 to 1868 at the Royal Institute for Deaf-Mutes in Milan. Afterwards she lived at the Mother House in Piacenza with her mother, who entrusted her to the care of a sister, and at times with her maternal grandparents in Genoa and, in summer, at Albaro. She was sometimes the guest of families who were friends of her mother: the Counts Marazzani, Altieri and others. At 23 she married Count Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei, whom she loved tenderly and who loved her in return. Mother Rosa stood by her and gave her much support in her task as mother and wife. She had six children: Maria Adelaide, Rosa, Camillo, Anna Federica, Emilia, Bernardo. She died in Rome aged 73, on 15 September 1926.

13. DECAVI (Fr.) LUIGI, born at Cesino (Pontedecimo - GE) on 26 August 1826. He came to know Mother Rosa and the Sisters of the Sampierdarena community in his ordinary ministry as curate of «S. Martino della Cella», in whose area the new work of the Daughters of Saint Anne had been started. He took the charitable institution to heart and, with helpful and attentive readiness, worked to further its smooth running and development, devoting himself especially to the spiritual direction of the girls.

He also worked for the opening of the house at Nizza Monferrato.

His correspondence with Mother Rosa and some of the Sisters runs from 1869 to 1872.

Later historical information about him is scarce. In 1881 Bishop Salvatore Magnasco appointed him parish priest of Fiorino, which he led for some twenty years. Cf. Arch St FSA G 27/5.

14. DONADIO (Father) AGOSTINO. Born at Morano Calabro (Cosenza) in 1830. Entering the Order of Minims very young, he made his novitiate at 17. He was ordained priest in Rome at the convent of S. Francesco di Paola ai Monti, where he served as Corrector (Superior) and Rector of the adjoining church. He was also General Councillor (1890-1906) and postulator of the causes of the Saints of the Order of Minims. He therefore dealt with those of Fr. Bernardo M. Clausi and Sr. Filomena of Santa Coloma, whose biographies he wrote and published.

Bound to Mother Rosa by deep friendship, he helped her considerably in the expansion of the Institute, especially in Rome and elsewhere. He was present at M. Rosa's death, having brought her the image of Mary Mater Gratiae venerated by Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi. He died on 31 August 1907 at the sanctuary of S. Francesco di Paola at Paola (Cosenza).

15 FRATEJACCI (Mgr.) GIAMBATTISTA. Auditor to Pius IX's Vicar, Card. Costantino Patrizi. Mother Rosa met him in Rome during her stay there for the founding of the Institute. Born at Vetralla (VT), he died in Rome on 3 September 1877.

  1. GAGGIA (Father) FRANCESCO. Born at Pellizzano di Trento on 21 November 1811. He entered the Congregation of the Mission at the Alberoni College (PC) on 21 October 1832, where he studied philosophy and moral theology. He was later Superior at Perugia and, from 1860 to 1880, at the Alberoni College. He then served as Visitor (= Provincial) until his death in Rome on 24 February 1882.

  2. GATTORNO FRANCESCO, father of Mother Rosa. Born in 1796. Through his tenacious industry and administrative shrewdness he made his way in business in Genoa and beyond. In 1827, at 31, he married Adelaide Campanella and was able to give his family, which grew to six children, an atmosphere of moral

serenity and great financial security. Respecting his daughter Rosa's choices, he appreciated the importance and sacrifices of her work, stood by her with moral support and, with prudent and careful advice, helped her in administrative difficulties. He died in Genoa in 1874.

18. GHISLANDI (Cav. Fr.) ELISEO, born in 1821, ordained priest in Milan in 1844. He devoted himself to the education and rehabilitation of the deaf. At the «Royal Institute for Deaf-Mutes Princes of Piedmont» in Milan (where Carlotta Custo, Mother Rosa's daughter, was educated) he was catechist-instructor from 1853 to 1863 and director from 1863 to 1888. Under his direction the oral method was adopted, so that at the International Congress of 1880 he was able to show the delegates that the old sign method of the Abbé de l'Épée had been superseded. Moved by humanitarian and pastoral passion and with the expertise of a lifetime devoted to the rehabilitation of deaf-mutes, he worked actively to set up private institutions that would give disabled young people, already taught in specialised schools, the chance to continue their formation in life-giving surroundings suited to their condition and particular needs; and that would at the same time support families, often unable to help their children take a dignified place in society.

He also approached Mother Rosa Gattorno about this, as the correspondence shows.

His publications deserve mention, especially those of fundamental importance in religious education: Il Catechismo ad uso dei Sordomuti and a Compendio di Storia Sacra ad uso dei Sordomuti.

1. CLAUSI (Father) BERNARDO MARIA, was born at S. Sisto dei Valdesi (CS) on 26 November 1789 and died at Paola (CS) on 20 December 1848, with a reputation for holiness widely known among the highest classes of society and still more among ordinary people.

In the deepest humility he lived the joy of encountering and ceaselessly seeking God, the sole reason for his life, and, like Christ on the cross, he experienced abandonment, entrusting and offering himself to him with «dark» faith, made still stronger by the trial, and with stronger love and will to give himself.

He belonged wholly to God and wholly to people. Constantly travelling in the ceaseless coming and going of charity, he answered the invitations of the «gentry» who counted for wealth and fame but who also needed comfort in the various forms of suffering that, by the law of universal human equality, strike the families of the rich as well as of the poor; who needed too to draw from his rough, clear gospel wisdom the light of counsel to discern well and act with justice, uprightness and goodness in the social responsibilities entrusted to them. And above all he, a son of the people, was among the people, the simple folk, bringing them, even through miracles, freedom from every kind of ill and awakening faith in God and veneration for «his Madonna», whom he carried everywhere in the image of the «Mother of Grace and Mercy».

No less fruitful, and awakening lively spiritual energies, was his presence in women's monasteries and religious institutes in Rome and other places in Italy.

Quite unique was his influence on the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, which owes him its specific charism. He had the inspiration to found a religious Family in the Church dedicated to Saint Anne, the Mother of Mary, and passed it on to Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore, who took up the legacy and, at the moment chosen by the Lord, carried it out, as he himself relates. When in Piacenza he met Rosa Gattorno, who with her first companions was beginning a religious Congregation, he sensed that she was the person chosen by God to bring to life the «dream» of the Venerable Father Bernardo.

Mother Rosa experienced personally Fr. Bernardo's decisive role. She accepted his clear and insistent inspiration to have the Rule

written by Fr. Tornatore; she received and venerated «his Madonna» as a sign of his benevolence and special love. She entrusted herself to the Mother of Grace and Mercy. She was always blessed by her and, during a very grave illness that had brought her to the point of death, was healed, apparently miraculously. And she entrusted her daughters to her. As an expression of gratitude, love and veneration she dedicated to her the church she had built beside the generalate in Rome, so that her gentle image might continue to be a sign and channel of God's grace and mercy towards his children. Cf. lett 43, 70, 149, 202, 212, 226, 229.

Cf. Bellantonio P. A., Bernardo Clausi, Post. Gen. dei Minimi, Rome, 1979.

2. COGROSSI (Fr.) LUIGI. Born at Colleone (Cremona) on 25 April 1806. He prepared for the priesthood at the Piacenza Seminary, was ordained priest also at Piacenza on 19 March 1831, and was assigned to his home diocese to minister at Colleone. A man of piety and pastoral zeal, he stood out and was talked about from his seminary days, not so much for these qualities, common to all who devote their lives to souls, nor for outstanding intelligence or learning. Rather, many considered him a «saint» because of the extraordinary powers of «healer» and «wonder-worker» he was said to have. He used this power freely on the sick who flocked to him, using water he had blessed. And some took advantage of his good faith for personal gain. The civil and religious authorities, seeing that the spontaneous influx of people, even from neighbouring villages, was turning into fanaticism and credulous popular religion, and that clashes between his enthusiastic supporters and rigid opponents were causing division and disturbing the village's normal life, sought remedies: first a warning from the parish priest, then from the Bishop, and finally his temporary removal from Colleone.

It is not known for certain where and how Rosa Gattorno met Fr. Luigi Cogrossi, probably in Genoa. From the correspondence with her «friends» and her parents he appears from 1864 as a mutual acquaintance. In 1865 he became her confessor and spiritual guide. He certainly encouraged her to found the new Institute and helped her actively. He accompanied her to Rome in January 1866, together with Teresa Porta, widow Morasso, and arranged her audience with Pius IX. He suggested to her the idea of a foundation in Piacenza and, helped by his old friendships, smoothed the way. Finally he worked in the enterprise as

«director» of the Mother House, where he normally lived, apart from some periods in Rome, until his removal, decided by Mother Rosa in August 1867 (cf. lett 21, 22, 23).

He then moved to Rome and died there on 19 February 1885, aged 79. Cf. lett 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 23.

3. RICCHINI (Fr.) ANGELO. Custodian of the church of Our Lady of Graces in the «Coscia» district of Sampierdarena, inhabited mostly by poor families. Sensitive to his people's problems and concerned for their human advancement, he had opened a free elementary school in rooms beside the church, entrusting it to two lay teachers, and wanted to found a boarding home for girls «at risk», to remove them from the bad influence of broken families. Hearing of what Rosa Gattorno had done in Piacenza, he agreed with her and Fr. Tornatore to set up a «grand» institute in Sampierdarena. He presented the girls who were the first residents of the work, begun at first in the inadequate rooms near the church, and gave 40,500 lire in Papal Credit bonds for its later establishment. But the large building the plan required could not be found. The Daughters of Saint Anne began small and continued in poverty and simplicity. Mother Rosa could find nothing better than to move the work to her father's villa, also in Sampierdarena, which she rented.

This difference of views and of what was done gave rise to the conflict between Fr. Angelo Ricchini and the Sisters, first with small objections and criticisms of their work, then with a demand for repayment of the sum he had given. Eventually it came to a dispute that ended in a lawsuit against Mother Rosa and Father Tornatore, concluded in 1877 in their favour. Fr. Angelo Ricchini died on 25.9.1878.

Cf. lett 83, 85, 88, 90, 94, 122, 132, 134, 135, 154, 175, 185, 188, 244.

4. TORNATORE (Father) GIOVANNI BATTISTA, of the Priests of the Mission. Born at Dolceacqua (Imperia) on 11 April 1820. He entered the Congregation at 16, took vows on 21 December 1838 and was ordained priest in Rome on 23 March 1844. From 1852 until his death he was in Piacenza at the Alberoni College, teaching fundamental and moral theology in turn. Widely known in Italy and abroad as a man of learning — he was distinguished for his studies and writings in theology and spirituality, so much so

as to be made a member of the Academy of Thomists — he was valued above all as a priest. The wisdom of the philosopher and the depth of the theologian, the austerity of the ascetic and the piety of the religious, and his simple, cordial goodness made him an eminent figure, appreciated and esteemed not only by his students and colleagues. Distinguished people in Piacenza and other cities sought him out as a spiritual guide.

On 25 March 1866 — he was 46 — he met Rosa Gattorno, a meeting prepared by Providence for them both. Sensing in her the person chosen by God to carry out the inspiration of Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi, he supported her plan, first introducing her to the «glorious Mother of Mary Immaculate» and guiding her as confessor in the ways of the Spirit.

His presence, occasional and almost external at first, gradually became that of a familiar figure, close, involved and jointly responsible for the beginning and growth of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne. At the Foundress's request he wrote its Rule, expressing in a single synthesis Mother Rosa's inspiration and his own, which received from the presence of Saint Anne the clear stamp of biblical spirituality.

He educated the Daughters of Saint Anne in the spirit of the Rule and was their guide, father, teacher and formator. His human and Christian richness as a good and upright man, and his presence as a learned and holy priest, gave the Daughters of Saint Anne that stamp of genuine spirituality which draws perennial relevance from biblical sources. The Father died in Piacenza on 31 January 1895.

IV. FOUNDATIONS (1866 to 1870)

1. PIACENZA, Mother House.

Rosa Gattorno arrived in Piacenza with her first five companions on 13 March 1866. They lodged temporarily in rented premises in Via Fodesta, today Via X Giugno. There the little group began community life, sharing life and prayer and practising charity by visiting and nursing the sick poor at home.

In May the community settled in the Palazzo Dal Verme, bought by the Foundress on 26 March of that year and adapted to the needs of the newborn institution, which, as the Foundress had charismatically sensed, took Most Holy Mary as its inspiration. They were in fact called «Daughters of Mary Immaculate and Minims of St. Francis of Assisi».

In the early days of the foundation they were helped by the priest Luigi Cogrossi, whom they had known for some years before the work began. As «director» he lived in the house, though not permanently, because of his journeys to Rome on personal business. A little over a year later, in the first half of August 1867, the Mother, having found him unreliable for reasons of temperament and religious fanaticism, dismissed him, informing the competent church authorities.

On arriving in Piacenza she had met Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, Priest of the Mission and professor of theology at the Alberoni College, who helped her so much that he is considered Co-founder.

Activities:

  • formation of postulants, novices, sisters

  • nursing cholera victims. As a hygienic precaution the 24 sisters assigned to the sick lived in a house they called «St. Francis», in Via Della Morte, now Via Gregorio X, which after the epidemic became the infirmary for sick sisters.

- education of boarding girls (mostly orphans of cholera victims), girls «in danger» and girls who had «fallen»

  • education of deaf-mute girls

  • weaving workshop for the boarding girls

2. CENTO, Hospital

The sisters began work on 2 February, together with the «Sons of Mary Immaculate» and under the same agreement made by them. To get round the recent suppression of religious institutions decreed by the Italian Government in 1866 and the very strong hostility of secularist circles to religious nursing the sick, the Sons presented themselves in lay dress as a lay association, the «Humanitarian Hospital Society». The Board had gladly accepted their offer, hoping they would end the chronic chaos in the hospital caused by the staff's widespread indifference to the proper running of services.

The «daughters» presented by Mother Rosa were given the nursing of the women's ward and the kitchen and linen-room services.

Once the work was under way, while both the brothers and the sisters tried to do their best, on the other side a cold war and hostility were being fed. Six months after the start, with the work going well, the Prefecture sent the Board a peremptory order to dismiss the «Hospitallers», on the «legal» grounds of «the need to rid oneself of persons suspected of being opposed to the established order», which in reality concealed other private motives of the staff who had been removed from the hospital for negligence and incompetence.

Mother Rosa's «Daughters», inspired by the spirit of charity, dedication and sacrifice in which she was forming them, enjoyed, as the Chief Physician declared, the full confidence of the Board, and were not covered by the expulsion decree, not being members of the «Humanitarian Society»; so they stayed on in the hospital, enduring a difficult situation. Several times the Mother had to go there to smooth out problems. When necessary she made proposals and lodged due protests. This went on for more than a year. Finally she submitted draft regulations reconciling the needs of the service with those of the community, but no agreement was reached. The sisters too were dismissed, and left the hospital in early May 1869.

3. SAMPIERDARENA, Orphanage-School

The work, proposed by Fr. Angelo Ricchini, a priest living in Sampierdarena, and accepted by Mother Rosa and Father Tornatore, began on 14 November 1868, when Mother Rosa arrived with the six Sisters who made up the community, one of whom,

Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, was superior. Their first premises were in the house of Signora Bodda, opposite the Church of Our Lady of Graces, of which Fr. Angelo Ricchini was Custodian. All agreed at once on the urgent need to find a building suitable for running and developing the work, but without success. They carried on in the same rooms, cramped and poor. The number of boarding girls grew. The following spring the work moved to the Villa Gattorno, also in Sampierdarena, rented from Mother Rosa's father.

At the beginning of 1869 three Sisters of the community, still under Superior Francesca, were sent to Genoa to Fr. Costantino Peragallo's institute, the «Retreat for girls in danger», Convent of S. Nicolò, Via S. Nicolò, to educate the boarding girls and teach them in the elementary school, which one of them directed.

Activities:

  • Education of the boarding girls and training in sewing and embroidery

  • Girls' elementary school, with a day section for boys as well

- visiting and nursing the sick at home, including at night.

In Fr. Peragallo's «Retreat»:

— education and teaching of the boarding girls in the attached elementary school.

4. PIACENZA. Boys' School

Opened on 20 November 1870 in municipal premises in Strada della Morte (now Gregorio X), formerly used as a Teacher Training School and Women's Workroom, lent by the City Council for nine years in response to the Foundress's request: «to take off the streets and educate the children and boys of the destitute class, aged four to thirteen». It was very well attended.

Activities:

  • Nursery school

  • Elementary school

  • Free meals for pupils

Virginia Si-nagra, pressantemente m'invitò a prendermi cura della Causa. Confesso di aver dubitato assai nel primo momento, ma, superate le iniziali titubanze e dubbi, accettai volentieri l'incarico postulatorio e mi tuffai, nel nome del Signore, nelle acque profonde della vita e l'opera di M. Gattorno, per tanti versi singolare, diventando subito un appassionato e sincero ammiratore di questa donna genovese dell'800, contemplativa e mistica, ma anche volitiva e dinamica.

Di conseguenza, essendo ora questi i miei rapporti con la Causa di M. Gattorno e con le sue figlie, non mi è stato facile negarmi all'invito fattomi dalla Rev.ma M. Sinagra, che mi chiedeva una breve presentazione del secondo volume dell'Epistolario della Fondatrice, sposa fedele nello stato del santo matrimonio, sacrificata mamma di famiglia, dinamica Fondatrice di un grande Istituto votato alla pratica poliedrica della carità cristiana, perfetta religiosa, costantemente tesa alla ricerca della via delle virtù, in continua ascesa nell'arduo cammino della santità.

Madre Gattorno, ai tempi in cui era in gestazione l'unità d'Italia, fu, nella sua perfetta linearità di vita cristiana in tutte le svariate vicende della sua esistenza, una testimone autentica dell'amore evangelico nel mondo. Una appassionata testimone dell'Invisibile. Testimone di Dio, ricco di misericordia, nel cuore del mondo, testimone, direi pure, del mondo nel cuore di Dio. Fu certo una donna pienamente inserita nel suo tempo— l'Italia risorgimentale dell'800— dotata però di un forte senso di trascendenza e di eternità. Una donna, infine, che visse la fede cristiana dalle radici del seno materno in famiglia fino al suo definitivo incontro con Dio il 6 maggio 1900, all'età di 69 anni.

Per questa donna che vivrà la sua fede senza tentennamenti di sor-

ta e con una radicalità ineccepibile, Dio mai fu una cifra o una figura geometrica più o meno decifrabile, ma ciò che è stato sempre e continuerà ad essere per i santi: una Realtà viva e palpitante, Qualcuno che irresistibilmente ci trascina, ci coinvolge, una Persona calorosa ed accogliente, la Persona del Padre, del Fratello, dell'Amico che ci ama e ci sollecita per completare accanto a Lui l'opera della salvezza.

La vita interiore di M. Gattorno, da giovane nel mondo, da sposa e madre in famiglia e da Fondatrice e anima consacrata in un Istituto di Carità, è stata perennemente e senza interruzione incentrata in Dio, scoperto ed amato come Padre, e in Gesù Cristo, Figlio di Dio, generosamente seguito fino alle ultime conseguenze nella pratica del perfetto amore, sulle orme della Madonna Immacolata, sotto il patrocinio di Sant'Anna.

Cosi M. Gattorno, piena di Dio e configurata a Gesù, alla scuola dì Maria Santissima e di Sant'Anna, apprese ad essere una donna per l'umanità. Direi anzi una donna voluta da Dio all'epoca dell'Italia del Risorgimento come impareggiabile testimone dei valori più alti della vita, apostola tutta di un pezzo, consumata dalla passione del Vangelo e dalla brama di evangelizzare, per quanto possibile, tutto il mondo. Prima di morire ebbe la gioia di vedere l'Istituto da lei fondato varcare i limiti d'Italia verso altri lontani orizzonti. Vide le sue figlie che salpavano trepidanti di apostolico zelo verso l'Europa, l'Africa e i paesi della lontana America.

Oggi, le figlie di questa grande e singolare Madre, forse per meglio aiutare tutti noi a prepararci all'evento della glorificazione della Serva di Dio, che immaginiamo non tanto lontana, ci offrono con questo secondo volume dell'Epistolario della Fondatrice, una nuova possibilità di conoscere più profondamente M. Gattorno e di penetrare quindi più ampiamente nei segreti della sua ricca spiritualità, traboccante di amore e di generoso spirito di materna donazione.

Con schietta sincerità devo confessare che sfogliando una dopo l'altra le numerose pagine di questo secondo volume dell'Epistolario dì M. Gattorno — pagine intime in cui si riflette al naturale e senza finzione lo spirito delicatamente materno di M. Rosa, pagine diafane come l'acqua chiara che sgorga dalla sorgente — mi sono sentito soggiogato dall'affascinante e travolgente personalità umana e mistica della Serva di Dio, sposa, mamma e Fondatrice dell'Istituto delle Figlie di Sant'Anna. Ho sentito in queste pagine il senso delicatamente umano di una Santa Teresa d'Avila e allo stesso tempo la calorosa ispirazione mistica della grande riformatrice del Carmelo.

Evidentemente, come potrà verificare il lettore di questo secondo

volume dell'Epistolario di M. Rosa, si tratta di una collezione di lettere scritte come risposta a tante necessità ed eventualità circostanziali e congiunturali; sono lettere scritte senza far troppa attenzione alle esigenze letterarie, anzi redatte con qualche imprecisione stilistica o con modalità talvolta dialettali. Ma tutto ciò si comprende e si spiega facilmente, tenuto conto della fretta con cui tante di queste lettere furono scritte, in una breve pausa del lavoro sempre urgente o, più spesso ancora, rubando un po' di sonno alla dose già ridotta dalle lunghe preghiere e dallo spirito di penitenza di M. Rosa.

È chiaro che le lettere di questo secondo volume dell'Epistolario sono diverse tra di loro per l'importanza del tema, il loro contenuto, la loro motivazione e scopo e la categoria o eventuali bisogni della persona o persone a cui sono indirizzate. Ma una cosa è ad ogni modo certa: non c'è nessuna lettera, grande o piccola, scritta dalla Serva di Dio che non abbia lo stesso filo conduttore; cioè il profondo senso di Dio, prima causa movente di tutte le azioni della Madre, e allo stesso tempo qualche cosa di sé stessa come messaggio materno: il profumo delle sue virtù che ancora oggi, leggendo attentamente le lettere che M. Gattorno scrive alle sue figlie o a tante persone da lei conosciute, spinge e stimola a proseguire anche noi sulla strada del bene e del vero amore, sotto la guida di una tale e tanto ispirata maestra.

Le lettere della M. Rosa, contenute in questo secondo volume, dirette quasi tutte ad anime elette, bramose di vivere la fede in profondità, sono un aiuto non soltanto per noi, per conoscere meglio l'alto livello della spiritualità di M. Rosa Gattorno, ma risultano anche per quanti avranno la fortuna di leggere e gustare l'Epistolario, un potente stimolo per progredire sempre più nelle vie del Signore verso le vette più alte della perfezione cristiana.

Vogliano Gesù, Maria e la gloriosa Madre Sant'Anna benedire lo sforzo realizzato dall'Istituto delle Figlie di Sant'Anna— al quale come Postulatore della Causa di Canonizzazione della Fondatrice mi sento spiritualmente legato — affinché tutte loro e con loro i moltissimi devoti ed ammiratori di M. Rosa, possano vivere generosamente fedeli allo spirito interiore ed apostolico ereditato dalla Serva di Dio e del quale le pagine di questo Epistolario sono una costante prova e stimolo.

P. Carlo Lizarraga, C.P.
